newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan United Micro sets T$500 bln wafer fab plan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan United Micro sets T$500 bln wafer fab plan.

text.p: Taiwan semiconductor maker United Microelectronics Corp said on Thursday it would build six advanced wafer fabrication plants in southern Tainan over 10 years at a cost of T$500 billion.

United Micro's ambitious expansion, announced in Taipei, is Taiwan's single biggest investment scheme to date, outstripping a huge T$400 billion wafer project that rival chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp announced in April.

The United Micro plant, like that of its rival, will be built in southern Taiwan's Tainan Science-based Industrial Park, a new development whose ambition is to challenge Taiwan's main high-tech manufacturing park at northern Hsinchu.
Taiwan Semiconductor and United Micro rank as Taiwan's number one and number two semiconductor makers.

In dollar terms, each project, once completed, will dwarf what until April was Taiwan's most ambitious investment project, a US$9 billion petrochemical plant being built in central Taiwan by Formosa Plastics group.

The United Microelectronics plan envisages building six advanced wafer fabrication plants, the first of which, budgeted at T$55 billion, is scheduled to go on line in 1999 with a capacity to produce 50,000 eight-inch wafers a month.

Once that project is running, United Micro plans to build five more wafer fabs, opening one every one or two years, that will be designed to make more advanced wafers measuring 12 inches or more at a rate of 20,000 wafers a month.

The wafer fab complex will produce what the company called "special application" microprocessors and other chips, a signal that United Micro is wooing the same custom-order foundry business that rival Taiwan Semiconductor has targetted.
"This will allow United Microelectronics to become the world's leading semiconductor wafer servicing company," the company said in a statement.
"With this advantage we hope to attract potential clients and make high value-added products for them," it added.
United Microelectronics chairman Robert Tsao said he believed the huge investment carried litle risk, as global demand for advanced semiconductors continues to grow.
"The investment risk will be low because the need for wafer technology will be very significant in the future," Tsao said at a news conference after announcing the huge project.
The company said it expected sales to reach T$500 billion in 2010 and that the new wafer complex would provide some 5,000 new jobs in Taiwan's fast-growing high-tech manufacturing sector.
As for financing the huge expansion, Tsao said United Micro's own current finances were "sufficient to finance the first stage of the plan" -- the eight-inch wafer fab.
"No problem," Tsao said briskly. He gave no details.

Tsao acknowledged that United Micro saw Taiwan Semicon as its main local rival, but described the competition in terms of intellectual prowess and creativity rather than more traditional measures of sales or output.
"Whichever company can get the most talented people will stand out in the competition," Tsao said.

Tsao declined to comment on persistent market rumours that Taiwan Semiconductor's former president, Donald Brooks, planned to sign on with United Micro. Brooks left Taiwan Semiconductor two months ago, citing family reasons.
-- Taipei newsroom, Kevin Chen (886-2-508-0815)
